title: Do More Doctors Mean Fewer Infant Deaths? A 154-Country Check
description: Physician density and infant mortality correlate at −0.73, one of the strongest links in global health data. The countries that break the pattern show why it isn't the whole story.

title: Does Money Buy Happiness? What the Country Data Actually Shows
description: Comparing GDP per capita against national happiness scores across 160 countries. Income explains about 41% of the gap — and the exceptions are more interesting than the rule.

title: Why Do Birth Rates Fall as Education Rises? The 150-Country Picture
description: Fertility and university enrolment correlate at −0.66 across 150 countries. South Korea now records 0.75 births per woman. What the data shows, and what it can't.

title: Healthcare Spending vs Life Expectancy: Why the Link Is Weaker Than You Think
description: Health spending as a share of GDP barely predicts how long people live — the correlation across 193 countries is just 0.18. Here is why the statistic misleads almost everyone.

title: How to Read Country Statistics Without Being Fooled
description: Six traps that make world rankings misleading — share-of-GDP ratios, inverted index scales, gross enrolment above 100%, and more. With worked examples from real datasets.

title: The Digital Divide in 2025: Internet Access vs National Income
description: Income predicts internet access far less well than it used to — a correlation of just 0.47 across 185 countries. Mobile networks broke the old relationship.

title: Press Freedom and Corruption: How Closely Do They Actually Track?
description: Across 170 countries the two indices correlate at −0.61. The Nordics sweep both ends. But both scores come from expert surveys, which complicates what the number means.

title: Why the World's 'Most Renewable' Countries Are Its Poorest
description: DR Congo gets 96% of its energy from renewables. Kuwait gets 0.1%. The statistic is real — and almost everyone reads it backwards.

title: Sanitation and Maternal Mortality: The Strongest Link in the Atlas
description: Access to basic sanitation and maternal death rates correlate at −0.80 across 184 countries — stronger than income, doctors or health spending. Why plumbing tracks survival.
